title: Polished vs unpolished rice: what milling takes off the grain
summary: What husking and polishing do to a rice grain, how unpolished rice cooks and keeps, and how HariLeaf mills its rice.
body:
Every grain of rice grows inside a husk. Under the husk is the bran — a thin brown or red layer — and the germ at one end of the grain. Inside is the white, starchy endosperm. How much of this the mill removes decides what ends up in your pot.

## What milling does

- **Husking** (also called hulling) takes off only the husk, which you can't eat. The grain keeps its bran and germ, so it looks brown or red and tastes nutty.
- **Polishing** goes further: the husked grain is rubbed against abrasive surfaces until the bran and germ are worn away, leaving the white endosperm. Some mills then give it a final gloss.

"Unpolished" rice is husked but not polished. "Polished" or white rice has had its bran and germ removed. Partly polished rice sits in between, so it's worth checking how far a rice was milled.

## How it changes cooking

- Unpolished rice takes longer to cook and needs a little more water, because the bran layer slows the water getting in. A 20–30 minute soak makes up most of the difference.
- It is chewier and more aromatic, and the grains hold their shape — good for khichdi, pulao and everyday dal-chawal.
- The bran contains oil, so unpolished rice keeps for less time than white rice. Store it airtight in a cool, dry place and use it before the best-before date on the pack.

## How HariLeaf mills its rice

We mill our rice only to remove the husk. We don't polish it, so the bran and germ stay on the grain. Every pack carries its batch code and packed-on date, and lab results appear on the product page as they come in. Read more about [how we grow, mill and grind](/our-process/).

## What we do and don't say

We list nutrition values only when we have measured them: each rice page shows its values per 100 g and where they come from. We don't make health claims about rice.
